tier_reason: The README and comparison/README.md carry go test -bench output against mattn/go-runewidth v0.0.23 and rivo/uniseg v0.4.7 (pinned in comparison/go.mod), produced by the public comparison/benchmark_test.go, with the CPU named (Apple M2, darwin/arm64). The Go toolchain version is not stated anywhere, so it falls short of A; first-party only, so C (same as other Go entries with an unstated toolchain).

corrections.claimed_speedup: README / comparison/README.md go test -bench output (Apple M2, darwin/arm64), displaywidth vs go-runewidth vs uniseg: String_Mixed 6085 vs 9970 vs 19060 ns/op; String_EastAsian 6118 vs 13917 vs 19263 ns/op; String_ASCII 54.54 ns/op (2347 MB/s) vs 125.5 ns/op (1020 MB/s) vs 1478 ns/op; String_Emoji 3265 vs 5110 vs 7137 ns/op; Rune_EastAsian 3454 vs 11432 ns/op; Rune_ASCII 255.5 vs 264.7 ns/op; TruncateWithTail 2495 vs 4569 ns/op; TruncateWithoutTail 2456 vs 5182 ns/op; 0 allocs except the with-tail truncation (14 allocs on both sides). Speedups over go-runewidth (derived from page data): 1.64x mixed strings, 2.27x East Asian, 2.30x ASCII, 1.57x emoji, 3.31x East Asian runes, 1.04x ASCII runes (parity), 1.83x and 2.11x truncation.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchmem in comparison/ with default gc build flags; the Go toolchain version is not stated (root go.mod declares go 1.18, but the pinned go-runewidth v0.0.23 declares go 1.23, so the comparison needs Go 1.23 or later)
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark; code is public (comparison/benchmark_test.go) and the CPU is named, but the Go toolchain version is not, and the README run is undated. Both sides do the same work (string/rune display width with default or East-Asian-ambiguous-wide settings, truncation to the same widths over the same test_cases.txt and string sets). go-runewidth now uses clipperhouse/uax29 (by the same author as displaywidth) for grapheme segmentation, so the gap comes mostly from width lookup, not segmentation. The baselines are Go libraries; go-runewidth (about 720 stars, the de facto Go terminal-width library) is a recognisable incumbent within Go, but ICU, HarfBuzz and FreeType are not involved. Display width is a text-layout primitive, not shaping. No C++ implementation is involved.

notes: Numbers match the README byte for byte; benchmark code calls displaywidth.String/Rune/TruncateString against runewidth.StringWidth/RuneWidth/Truncate and uniseg.StringWidth on identical inputs. MIT license, not a fork, not archived, 19 stars, last commit 2026-05-17 (active).

tier_reason: README table compares hypher with the hyphenation crate on Apple M1, and the Criterion source is public (bench/bench.rs, bench/Cargo.toml: criterion 0.3, hyphenation 0.8 with embed_all), but the rustc version and profile flags are not stated and the run is undated; first-party, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (Apple M1): hyphenating 'extensive' (English) 356 ns vs 698 ns for hyphenation; 'διαμερίσματα' (Greek) 503 ns vs 1121 ns; loading English patterns 0 us vs 151 us; loading Greek patterns 0 us vs 0.826 us. Speedups 1.96x English and 2.23x Greek (derived from page data). The hypher load figures are not measured: bench.rs has no hypher load benchmark, and 0 us reflects the design (embedded automata used in place, no decoding), while the hyphenation side times Standard::from_embedded deserialization.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 142 stars, 20 forks; 3.28M crates.io downloads (1.43M recent); hosted in the typst organisation
corrections.caveats: Two single-word micro-benchmarks on one machine; Criterion source is public (bench/bench.rs) but the rustc version and flags are not stated and the README run is undated, so tier C. The word benchmarks do the same work on both sides (hyphenate one word with English and Greek patterns, drain the syllable or break iterator); hyphenation uses EnglishUS and GreekMono patterns. The pattern-loading rows are not a like-for-like measurement: hypher's 0 us is a design property, not a timed run. The baseline is the hyphenation crate (0.8.4, last released 2021-08-19, 1.15M crates.io downloads, 58 stars), the long-standing Rust Knuth-Liang hyphenation crate and a recognisable incumbent within Rust; it is not HarfBuzz, FreeType or ICU. Hyphenation is a text-layout step, not shaping. Pattern files in patterns/ carry their own licenses (LPPL, MPL, MIT, BSD-3) and are embedded into the binary.

notes: Numbers match the README; bench.rs times hypher::hyphenate against hyphenation::Standard::hyphenate on the same words. License MIT OR Apache-2.0 (Cargo.toml), not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-09-17 (version bump to 0.1.8), active.

tier_reason: PR #550 on github.com (merged 2026-07-30, shipped in v3.1.0) carries full per-script tables of SixLabors.Fonts vs HarfBuzzSharp on .NET 8.0.29 and .NET 10.0.10, produced by the public ShapeTextBenchmark.cs under the Gate config, but it names no CPU model, OS or BenchmarkDotNet version; first-party, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: PR #550 tables, .NET 10.0.10, mean time Fonts vs HarfBuzzSharp (ratio Fonts over HarfBuzz, derived from page data where the page gives only times): Latin 2.6744 vs 2.2843 us (1.17x); Arabic 4.9651 vs 3.9115 us (1.27x); Hebrew 4.5843 vs 4.6725 us (0.98x); Thai 4.2530 vs 3.9104 us (1.09x); Hangul 0.9258 vs 0.5645 us (1.64x); Devanagari 7.7347 vs 9.3177 us (0.83x); Khmer 4.1790 vs 3.7335 us (1.12x); Myanmar 25.2861 vs 22.9402 us (1.10x); Myanmar Zawgyi 0.7797 vs 0.8248 us (0.95x); Balinese 2.6941 vs 3.0572 us (0.88x). Faster on Devanagari (1.20x), Balinese (1.13x), Zawgyi (1.06x) and Hebrew (1.02x, near parity); slower on the other six, up to 1.64x slower on Hangul. The PR says seven of ten workloads are within 12% of HarfBuzz or faster; the release post reportedly counts three outright wins. On .NET 8.0.29 Fonts is faster only on Balinese (0.96x) and slower elsewhere (1.01x to 1.97x). Zero managed allocations per shape in steady state.
corrections.license: Six Labors Split License 1.0 (non-OSI: Apache-2.0 only for open-source or source-available use, transitive dependencies, non-profits and for-profits under 1M USD annual revenue; commercial license otherwise)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet Gate job (3 launches, 5 warmup, 15 iterations, /p:DebugType=portable) on the host runtime, net10.0 target (also run on .NET 8.0.29 per the PR); HarfBuzzSharp 14.2.1.1 with OpenType font functions; BenchmarkDotNet version not stated on the PR
corrections.caveats: First-party; numbers are on PR #550 (read through github.com) with no CPU model, OS or BenchmarkDotNet version, and the sixlabors.com release post was not opened (blocked). Not faster overall: on .NET 10 it beats HarfBuzz on three or four of ten scripts (Hebrew is near parity) and trails on six, up to 1.64x on Hangul and 1.27x on Arabic; on .NET 8 it wins only Balinese. Same work in principle (one short run of 25-60 characters per script, same font bytes, glyph advances summed), but the HarfBuzz side also pays several .NET-to-native interop calls and HarfBuzz's GuessSegmentProperties per iteration while Fonts is handed the direction, which weighs most on the sub-microsecond Hangul and Zawgyi runs. The baseline is native HarfBuzz through HarfBuzzSharp, a recognisable incumbent and in the list. The library is C#, not C++, and the non-OSI Split License makes it reference only.
